faq.q: How does a gravity dam work?
faq.a: A gravity dam holds back water simply by being heavy. Its weight presses it onto the rock so it cannot slide, and its wide base stops it tipping over.
asks: How do dams hold back water?

faq.q: Why are dams thicker at the bottom?
faq.a: Water pressure increases with depth: 10 metres down it is about one extra atmosphere, and 100 metres down about ten. So the bottom of a dam must resist far more push than the top.
asks: Why is water pressure higher at the bottom?

faq.a: Friction between the dam's base and the rock. The heavier the dam, the harder it presses down and the greater that friction, and the base is often keyed into the rock as well.
asks: Why doesn't the water push the dam away?

faq.q: What is the difference between a gravity dam and an arch dam?
faq.a: A gravity dam resists water by its own weight, so it is very thick. An arch dam curves upstream and pushes the water's force sideways into the canyon walls, so it can be much thinner.

faq.q: What is uplift under a dam?
faq.a: Water seeping into cracks under a dam pushes upward, partly lifting it and reducing its grip on the rock. Grout curtains and drainage holes keep this uplift small.
asks: Why do dams have drains in their base?

facts: Water pressure rises by about one atmosphere, roughly 100 kilopascals, for every 10 metres of depth.
Grand Coulee Dam in Washington State is one of the largest concrete gravity dams, containing about 9 million cubic metres of concrete.
